llm_response.content:
Empirical Research Plan: 608 Indonesian KDP Villages, 2003-04

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Primary strategy: Two separate village-level instrumental-variables (IV) designs.

A.  Audit probability → corruption  
   • 1st stage: predicted probability of an external BPKP audit.  
   • 2nd stage: effect of (endogenous) “audit actually occurred” on percent-missing.

B.  Community monitoring intensity → corruption  
   • 1st stage: predicted meeting attendance rate.  
   • 2nd stage: effect of (endogenous) “high participation” on percent-missing.

Why IV?  
• Audit visits and community attendance are both choice/endogenous: high-risk villages may be targeted for audit; elites may discourage attendance when they plan to steal.  
• Plausible, externally-given sources of exogenous variation are available (see instruments below).  
• Panel length (≤1 year) rules out DID/event study; no sharp cutoff for RDD.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  External Audit Arm  
   • Treatment variable (T_A): =1 if the village road project was audited by BPKP during implementation (Sept-03–Aug-04), 0 otherwise.  
   • Control:  villages not audited in that window.  
   • Timing: audit date ∈ project period; outcomes measured at completion.  
   • Instrument Z_A: predicted audit propensity based on (i) inverse road distance to nearest BPKP regional office, (ii) number of other KDP projects in the office’s catchment that year (work-load shifters), and (iii) whether the kecamatan randomly fell into the provincial “intensified-audit” rota in 2004Q1 (administrative scheduling information obtained from BPKP plan documents).

B.  Community-Monitoring Arm  
   • Treatment variable (T_M): =1 if ≥10% of village adults (≈250 persons) attend the key accountability meeting (“high participation”), 0 otherwise.  
   • Control: villages below that threshold.  
   • Instrument Z_M: exogenous determinants of meeting turnout  
        – Rain shock: cumulative rainfall (mm) during the scheduled meeting day measured at nearest BMKG weather station.  
        – Meeting-day clash with major Islamic holiday (binary).  
   These affect ability to attend but not corruption directly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Instrument relevance: Z_A strongly predicts actual audit; Z_M strongly predicts turnout.  
     Plausible: distance/work-load highly correlated with audit; rain/holiday suppress attendance.

A2. Exclusion restriction: Instruments affect percent-missing only through their effect on audits/attendance.  
     – Distance or rain should not mechanically change material/labor theft except via oversight; plausible given short time span and road-project homogeneity.  
     – Test by showing instruments uncorrelated with pre-project village characteristics.

A3. Independence (as-good-as-random): Conditional on controls, Z_A and Z_M are orthogonal to unobservables affecting corruption.

A4. Monotonicity: Moving closer to BPKP cannot make a village less likely to be audited; rain cannot increase turnout. Reasonable.

A5. SUTVA: One village’s audit or meeting turnout does not change another village’s corruption (block-grant funds not fungible across villages).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Threat 1 – Exclusion violation (distance may correlate with monitoring ability or material prices).  
  • Include kecamatan fixed effects + rich controls (transport cost index, material price level, road length).  
  • Conduct placebo test: run IV on pre-KDP village budget outcomes (1999 road projects) where no audits occurred.

Threat 2 – Weak instruments (especially Z_M).  
  • Report first-stage F-statistics.  
  • Combine rain and holiday dummies; use LIML as robustness.  
  • If weak, supplement with additional instrument: unanticipated death of village head (forces rescheduling/turnout shock).

Threat 3 – Non-compliance / measurement error in treatment.  
  • Cross-validate audit status with BPKP archives; code partial audits.  
  • Use shake-divert method to bound estimates (Lewbel 2021) if misclassification suspected.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# --------------------- 0. Packages ---------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(fixest)       # IV regression
library(modelsummary) # tables
# --------------------- 1. Load data --------------------
kg  <- fread("key_informant.csv")      # village covariates
mtg <- fread("meeting_survey.csv")     # attendance
hh  <- fread("household_survey.csv")   # perceptions (for controls)
eng <- fread("engineering_survey.csv") # actual quantities
acct<- fread("accountability_reports.csv") # reported spending
audit <- fread("bpkp_audit_status.csv")     # audit dates
weather <- fread("rain_daily_station.csv")  # rain
dist <- fread("distance_to_bpkp.csv")       # km

# --------------------- 2. Merge & Construct ------------
dt <- Reduce(function(x,y) merge(x,y,by="village_id",all=TRUE),
             list(kg,mtg,hh,eng,acct,audit,weather,dist))

# Actual vs reported spend
dt[, log_actual_mat  := log(actual_material_exp)]
dt[, log_report_mat  := log(reported_material_exp)]
dt[, percent_missing_mat := 100*(log_report_mat - log_actual_mat)]

dt[, log_actual_labor:= log(actual_labor_exp)]
dt[, log_report_labor:= log(reported_labor_exp)]
dt[, percent_missing_labor := 100*(log_report_labor - log_actual_labor)]

# Treatments
dt[, T_A := as.integer(audit_occured == 1)]
dt[, turnout_rate := attendees/eligible_adults]
dt[, T_M := as.integer(turnout_rate >= .10)]

# Instruments
dt[, Z_A := 1/dist_km]                          # inverse distance
dt[, Z_A2:= workload_inverse]                   # office work-load
dt[, Z_M1:= rain_mm]                            # rainfall on meeting day
dt[, Z_M2:= holiday_clash]                      # =1 if meeting on holiday

# Controls
ctrls <- c("road_length_km","pop_density","avg_income","implementation_team_education")

# --------------------- 3. Main IV specifications -------
# (a) Audit effect
iv_audit <- feols(percent_missing_mat ~ 1 | village_id | 
                  T_A ~ Z_A + Z_A2, data=dt,
                  cluster = ~kecamatan_id, controls = ctrls)
# (b) Community monitoring effect
iv_mon   <- feols(percent_missing_mat ~ 1 | village_id | 
                  T_M ~ Z_M1 + Z_M2, data=dt,
                  cluster = ~kecamatan_id, controls = ctrls)

# --------------------- 4. Robustness: alternative outcome
iv_audit_labor <- update(iv_audit, percent_missing_labor ~ .)
# Weak-instrument robust
iv_mon_liml <- feols(percent_missing_mat ~ 1 | village_id | 
                     T_M ~ Z_M1 + Z_M2, data=dt, 
                     iv_method = "liml", cluster=~kecamatan_id)

modelsummary(list("Materials theft" = iv_audit,
                  "Labor theft"     = iv_audit_labor,
                  "Community LIML"  = iv_mon_liml))
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results (Priors)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Economic theory (Becker crime model + monitoring):  
• External audits raise expected probability of detection → should reduce theft.  
• Community participation adds social sanctions and information spill-over → also reduces theft, but may be less powerful for materials (harder for laypeople to monitor sand/gravel volumes) than for labor (villagers observe who worked).

Qualitative prior magnitudes (percent-missing measured in log points):  
• Audit: −15 pp on materials, −10 pp on labor.  
• High participation: −5 pp on materials, −12 pp on labor.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV design) (1 = met, 0 = unsure)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1  Instrument relevance (first-stage F>10):                     1  
C2  Exclusion restriction plausibility:                          0.5  
C3  Independence / as-good-as-random given controls:             0.5  
C4  Monotonicity (no defiers):                                   1  
C5  SUTVA (no cross-village spillovers within study period):     1  
Total: 4/5 – acceptable but exclusion and independence will be scrutinised.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
End of Plan
